stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan brews over Bay of Bengal: What you need to know
stories.title: Cyclone Akvan brews over Bay of Bengal: What you need to know
stories.summary: Cyclone Akvan may intensify into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal by Tuesday (November 17, 2026)
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A weather system brewing over the Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the coming days, according to the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD).

The system has intensified into a Cyclonic Storm and is on Monday (November 16, 2026) evening, and is moving north-northwestwards towards Andhra Pradesh and has been named ‘Akvan’, a name suggested by Iran under the North Indian Ocean naming list, once it strengthens into a cyclonic storm.
What is Cyclone Akvan’s current trajectory?
It originated as a well-marked low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal on Saturday (November 14, 2026), the system intensified into a depression by Sunday (November 15, 2026) morning.

The storm may continue to move north-northwestwards and intensify into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal by Tuesday (November 17, 2026) evening and may cross the A.P. coast around noon on November 20, as a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm, with windspeed gusting to 145 kmph, similar to that of Arnab.
The system is forecast to bypass Tamil Nadu and move toward the Andhra Pradesh coast around November 19, 2026, also impacting Odisha.
Heavy rainfall warnings have been issued for coastal Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Andaman and Nicobar Islands through November 20, 2026.

In West Bengal, heavy rain is forecast for South 24 Parganas and Purba Medinipur from November 19 to 21, 2026, with downpour likely in the southern districts of Howrah, Paschim Medinipur and Jhargram on November 20 and 21.
According to the IMD, thunderstorms, accompanied with winds up to 40 kmph in Kolkata and most districts of Gangetic West Bengal is also likely.
A nip in the air over South Bengal is likely to dissipate as day and night temperatures will rise by two to three degrees Celsius from November 18, 2026, it said.
Cyclone Akvan is expected to cause rains in north coastal districts in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal area, it said.
Along the north Andhra coast, at Visakhapatnam Fishing Harbour, the Fisheries Department and Indian Coast Guard have recalled trawlers and halted marine operations.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan: Andhra Home Minister Anitha puts coastal districts on high alert, warns fishermen
stories.title: Cyclone Akvan: Andhra Home Minister Anitha puts coastal districts on high alert, warns fishermen
stories.summary: Andhra Pradesh Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha asks people to stay alert over the next four days and the Agriculture Department to help farmers protect crops ready for harvest
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The State government has stepped up its preparedness to deal with Cyclone Akvan over the Bay of Bengal.
Andhra Pradesh Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha directed officials to take precautionary measures in all coastal districts to prevent loss of life and property.

At a review meeting with officials of the Disaster Management Authority and the Real Time Governance Society on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), she asked District Collectors and Superintendents of Police in coastal districts to work in close coordination and remain on high alert.
Officials informed her that Cyclone Akvan was likely to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday evening and a very severe cyclonic storm by Thursday morning.
It was likely to cross the coast between Nellore and Tuni on Friday afternoon, they said.
The cyclone was expected to bring strong winds to coastal Andhra Pradesh on Thursday and Friday, accompanied by extremely heavy rainfall in some areas and heavy to very heavy rainfall in others.

Ms. Anitha said the government had successfully handled two cyclones in the past through coordinated efforts and called on all departments to demonstrate the same preparedness in dealing with the impending weather system.
She said the administration should provide assurance to people during the crisis, with officials remaining accessible on the ground and continuously monitoring the situation.
Appealing to people to remain alert over the next four days, she warned fishermen against venturing into the sea under any circumstances.
Residents of coastal areas were advised to monitor weather conditions and take necessary precautions.

She also asked the Agriculture Department to guide farmers on protecting crops ready for harvest from rain and strong winds, and to ensure that precautionary measures were followed during agricultural operations.
The Home Minister directed all government departments to work in coordination in the cyclone-affected areas and ensure that the administrative machinery was fully prepared to handle any emergency.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan to bring light rains for Chennai and surroundings on November 17
stories.title: Cyclone Akvan to bring light rains for Chennai and surroundings on November 17
stories.summary: The deep depression over Southeast and adjoining Southwest Bay of Bengal moved north-northwestwards and intensified into a cyclonic storm and lay centred at 5:30 p.m. about 610 km east of Chennai
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Cyclone Akvan was edging closer to the Andhra Pradesh coast on Thursday morning, slowly gathering muscle over the Bay of Bengal as the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast further intensification into a very severe cyclonic storm, potentially putting it in the league of its predecessor, Arnab.
At 5.30 am on Thursday, Akvan was positioned over the central parts of the south and adjoining west-central Bay.
It was closest to Chennai, at 610 km to its east, and farthest from Gopalpur in Odisha, at 790 km to its south.
Other reference points placed it 630 km north-east of Trincomalee in Sri Lanka; 660 km south-east of Machilipatnam; and 670 km south-south-east of Visakhapatnam.
The storm was making painfully slow headway, crawling north-northwestwards at barely 3 km an hour.
Its position had consequently changed little over the preceding six hours, even as its internal structure continued to organise and strengthen.
Akvan is expected to maintain its north-northwestward course, intensifying into a severe cyclone over the west-central Bay by Tuesday evening, according to the forecast timeline.
It is then expected to veer more towards the north-west, bringing it on a trajectory towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, before graduating into a very severe cyclonic storm around Thursday morning.
The IMD expects Akvan to continue its north-westward march and cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni around Friday noon.
It is forecast to make landfall as a very severe cyclonic storm, packing maximum sustained winds of 120-130 km/hr and gusts reaching 145 km/hr.

Meanwhile, a flight from Mumbai to Kochi on Monday evening offered an unusual ringside view of a spectacular cloudscape over the Konkan-Kanara coast, raising an intriguing possibility: the expanding atmospheric circulation of Akvan may have had a hand in the display, even from well over 1,000 km away.
The observation came from the left-hand side of the aircraft at cruising altitudes of 32,000-35,000 ft, around 6 pm.

stories.headline: ONGC well gas leak causes panic in Andhra Pradesh district
stories.title: ONGC well gas leak causes panic in Andhra Pradesh district
stories.summary: Kakinada (Andhra Pradesh), Nov 17 : A massive gas leak occurred from an ONGC gas drilling well in Andhra Pradesh’s Dr B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema district on Tuesday, triggering panic among people in surrounding villages. The gas leak from the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) rig occurred near Geddada village in Mamidikuduru mandal. According to officials, the gas began leaking around 4:30 a.m. on Tuesday, accompanied by a loud noise, and is currently spewing out in large volumes. The incident triggered panic among residents and commuters on the National Highway 216. Gas was reportedly spreading to nearby villages, with residents complaining of a strong gas smell. People living in the vicinity and motorists passing through the highway ran to safety after noticing the gas leak. Police halted vehicular movement on the Geddada-Mamidikuduru highway as a precautionary measure. ONGC officials and police were alerted, while specialised teams were being mobilised to contain the leak. A control team from Narsapur left for the spot to contain the blowout. The officials stated that there have been no fires so far and that the wellhead remains secure. ONGC personnel were taking measures to prevent the gas from spreading near the ground level. Fire-fighters arranged the water umbrella around the rig to prevent fire. Meanwhile, Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu has spoken with officials regarding a gas leak incident. He directed that residents in the affected areas be evacuated to safer locations. The Chief Minister said public safety must be given the highest priority. He said ONGC must take immediate action, deploying specialised technical teams to bring the gas leak under control. Noting that such incidents have occurred frequently of late, the Chief Minister instructed officials to immediately engage with ONGC management. He has ordered a review of safety protocols in consultation with the ONGC Chairman and other senior officials of the organisation. Authorities have already evacuated residents living within a one-kilometre radius of the gas well. As a precautionary safety measure, diesel generators and other equipment have been shut down and removed from the vicinity. A cementing team is arriving at the site to completely plug the gas well leak. ONGC officials have stated that the gas leak incident will be brought fully under control within the next 4-5 hours. (IANS)

stories.headline: FM holds third pre-Budget consultation with manufacturing experts
stories.title: FM holds third pre-Budget consultation with manufacturing experts
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 17 : Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Tuesday chaired the third pre-Budget consultation meeting with experts and industry leaders from the manufacturing sector as the government continued its stakeholder outreach ahead of the Union Budget 2027-28. According to the Finance Ministry, the meeting brought together representatives from the manufacturing industry to discuss sector-specific concerns, growth opportunities and policy measures that could be considered in the forthcoming Budget. The consultation was attended by senior government officials, including the secretaries of the Department of Economic Affairs, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), the Ministry of Mines and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, along with Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran, the ministry wrote on X. The latest meeting forms part of the Finance Ministry's annual pre-Budget exercise to gather inputs from key sectors of the economy before finalising Budget proposals. The manufacturing-sector discussions follow a series of consultations chaired by FM Sitharaman earlier in the week. On Monday, the Finance Minister held the second pre-Budget consultation with experts and stakeholders from the agriculture and rural development sectors. The discussions focused on measures to strengthen rural growth, boost farm incomes and enhance the contribution of agriculture to the broader economy. The meeting was attended by senior officials from the Department of Economic Affairs, the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. Earlier on the same day, the finance minister chaired the first round of consultations with leading economists, seeking views on macroeconomic trends, growth prospects and policy priorities for the upcoming fiscal year. In addition, the government has also been engaging with industry bodies as part of the consultation process. In recent interactions with the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PHDCCI), industry representatives called for customs duty rationalisation on key industrial raw materials and energy inputs to improve India's competitiveness as a manufacturing hub. (IANS)

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu government cannot ban transportation of minerals to other States, rules Madras High Court
stories.title: Tamil Nadu government cannot ban transportation of minerals to other States, rules Madras High Court
stories.summary: Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan declare as unconstitutional Rule 3A of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Illegal Mining, Tansportation and Storage of Minerals and Mineral Dealers Rules, 2011
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in summary weight 25.2
article_sentences: The Madras High Court on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) declared as unconstitutional Rule 3A of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Illegal Mining, Transportation and Storage of Minerals and Mineral Dealers Rules, 2011 which empowers the Director of Geology and Mining to impose a temporary ban on transportation of minerals to other States.

First Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan held that the rule, inserted by way of an amendment on July 9, 2026, was unconstitutional and also ultravires the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulations) Act, 1957, a central legislation under which the rules had been framed.

Consequentially, the judges also quashed an order passed by the Director of Geology and Mining on July 27, 2026 imposing a temporary ban on transportation of rough stones and their aggregates to other States, except to Puducherry and the Karaikal region for a period of three months, that was later extended by another three months from October 27, in order to ensure adequate availability in Tamil Nadu.

The orders were passed on a batch of writ petitions filed both in the principal seat of the High Court in Chennai as well as its Madurai Bench challenging the constitutional validity of Rule 3A introduced through an amendment to the statutory rules on July 9, 2026 as well as the consequential temporary ban order passed by the Director of Geology and Mining.

However, a host of crusher and quarry owners associations as well as individual owners of such facilities had approached the High Court contending that the newly-introduced statutory rule was ultravires Articles 301 (Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India) and 304(b) (power of a State legislature to impose reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse in public interest).

The petitioners had also contended that the statutory rule was ultravires Section 23(C)(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, a central legislation which empowers the State governments to frame rules for preventing illegal mining, transportation and storage of minerals.

Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan declare as unconstitutional Rule 3A of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Illegal Mining, Tansportation and Storage of Minerals and Mineral Dealers Rules, 2011.

The orders were passed on a batch of writ petitions filed both in the principal seat of the High Court in Chennai as well as its Madurai Bench challenging the constitutional validity of Rule 3A introduced through an amendment to the statutory rules on July 9, 2026 as well as the consequential temporary ban order passed by the Director of Geology and Mining.

First Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan held that the rule, inserted by way of an amendment on July 9, 2026, was unconstitutional and also ultravires the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulations) Act, 1957, a central legislation under which the rules had been framed.

article_sentences: The Centre, the RBI and the SEBI informed the Court of various measures taken to enable heirs to trace and claim the deposits.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (November 17) reserved its order on a public interest litigation filed by financial journalist Sucheta Dalal seeking a centralised, searchable database to help legal heirs trace unclaimed financial assets of deceased persons.

A bench comprising Justice Vikram Nath and Justice R Mahadevan heard Advocate Prashant Bhushan for the petitioner, Additional Solicitor General N Venkataraman for the Centre, Senior Advocate Dama Seshadri Naidu for the Reserve Bank of India and Advocate Amarjeet Singh Bedi for the Securities and Exchange Board of India.
During the hearing, ASG Venkataramani, for the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, referred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) and the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF).
He added that under the Companies Act, every company is obligated to make a disclosure regarding unclaimed deposits.
The public can access the disclosures made by companies through the portal of the IEPF authority.
Over 3 lakh claims have been processed till March 2026, and only 10% claims are pending, he said.
The amount of unclaimed dividends transferred during 2025-26 is 52.85 crores, and the total number of shares transferred during the said period is 3.58 crores.
The ASG said that these measures fulfil the prayers sought in the petition.
Regarding the steps taken by the Department of Financial Services, the ASG said that Section 26 of the Banking Regulation Act deals with unclaimed deposits.
Further, policy measures have been adopted to ease the processing of claims.
After the 2025 Banking Laws Amendment Act, up to four persons can be nominated.

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has dismissed the Uttar Pradesh government's appeal against relief granted to Azam Khan and extended the stay on conviction to his wife and son in the fake birth certificate case.

In a significant development in the fake birth certificate case involving Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Azam Khan and his family, the Supreme Court on Tuesday dismissed an appeal filed by the Uttar Pradesh government challenging the relief granted to the politician.
The court also extended relief to Khan's wife, Tazeen Fatima, and son, Abdullah Azam Khan, by staying their convictions.
A bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu dismissed the state's challenge and granted Fatima and Abdullah relief similar to the one previously extended to Khan.
The case dates back to allegations that Abdullah had obtained two birth certificates carrying different dates of birth.
While one certificate recorded his date of birth as January 1, 1993, the other mentioned September 30, 1990.
On October 18, 2023, a Rampur MP-MLA court convicted Azam Khan, Fatima and Abdullah in the case and sentenced all three to seven years in prison.
The family subsequently approached the Allahabad High Court seeking relief against the conviction.
In May 2024, the High Court stayed Khan's conviction and sentence but declined to grant similar relief to his wife and son.
The Uttar Pradesh government then moved the Supreme Court, challenging the relief granted to Khan.
The state's appeal has now been dismissed, while Fatima and Abdullah have also secured a stay on their convictions.
However, the Supreme Court's order does not amount to an acquittal.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court has sought a status report from the investigating agency probing the circumstances surrounding the death of Delhi Judicial Service officer Aman Sharma, whose demise was reported as a suspected suicide.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the direction on November 6 while hearing a suo motu case initiated by the Court to examine the circumstances leading to Sharma's death.
The Court has appointed Senior Advocate Haripriya Padmanabhan as amicus curiae to assist it in the proceedings.
"Meanwhile, the Investigating Agency is directed to file the status report," the Bench ordered, issuing notice returnable on December 7.
Sharma, aged 30, was found dead at his residence in Delhi's Safdarjung Enclave on May 2.
He had joined the Delhi Judicial Service on June 19, 2021, after completing his law degree from Symbiosis Law School, Pune.
During his tenure, Sharma served as a Judicial Magistrate First Class and Civil Judge, handling various criminal and civil matters.
From October 2025, he was functioning as the Secretary of the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) for North East District at the Karkardooma Courts.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Clears Lulu Mall's Resolution Plan For Manjeera Retail Holdings
stories.title: Supreme Court Clears Lulu Mall's Resolution Plan For Manjeera Retail Holdings
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday (November 16) has paved the way for the implementation of the resolution plan submitted by Lulu International Shopping Malls Private Limited for Manjeera Retail Holdings Private Limited, by dismissing as time-barred appeals challenging its approval.

A bench of Justice Sanjay Kumar and Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva held that the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) could not have entertained the appeals filed beyond the maximum 45-day period prescribed under Section 61(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC).
Lulu International had emerged as the successful resolution applicant after its plan received 100% approval from the Committee of Creditors.
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Hyderabad, approved the resolution plan on March 26, 2025.
Lulu International stated that it had invested ₹271.52 crore towards its implementation.

Three individuals who had entered into agreements to purchase commercial units in Manjeera Mall, Hyderabad challenged the approval, alleging that their payments towards the full sale consideration had been wrongly classified as “advances from customers” instead of recognising them as claims of financial creditors.
Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, an appeal against an NCLT order must be filed within 30 days, with a maximum additional 15 days available for condonation of delay.
In this case, the extended 45-day period expired on May 10, 2025, a second Saturday.
The respondents filed their appeals on May 11, 2025.

The NCLAT condoned the delay by applying Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which permits filing on the next working day when the court is closed on the last day of the prescribed limitation period.
Setting aside this order, the judgment authored by Justice Sanjay Kumar relied on its decision in Tata Steel Ltd.
Raj Kumar Banerjee 2025 LiveLaw (SC) 542, which clarified that Section 4 of the Limitation Act cannot extend the additional period available for condonation of delay under a special statute.

The district administration will take care of the evacuees' lunch and dinner, who were moved to a safe place.
Reassuring residents that the situation is under control, Ravirala said the gas is dispersing vertically rather than horizontally.

stories.headline: The Home-Grown Paradox
stories.title: The Home-Grown Paradox
stories.summary: TECHNOLOGY & NATIONAL SECURITY Imagine a defence office being told it can no longer use ChatGPT, Gemini or any other foreign AI tool. Only Indian-made AI is allowed. That may soon be real. On 9 November, Business Standard reported that the Centre is likely to push government-run critical sectors, especially defence and aerospace, towards home-grown AI models. One official told the paper that departments could be asked to avoid foreign frontier AI altogether. No ministry has confirmed this on record, and no order has been issued. The idea is easy to like. Why should India’s secrets pass through tools owned by American or Chinese companies? But there is a catch. A rule meant to make us safer could leave our most important offices with weaker tools, while the real weak point stays exactly where it was. What India has built so far The government’s IndiaAI Mission has a budget of about ₹10,372 crore. Under it, 20 AI models from 12 Indian startups have been approved, according to the same report. Some are already out: models from Sarvam and BharatGen, Soket’s EKA-1, and ZenteiQ’s Dhir models. This is real progress. The armed forces are also building their own AI systems that run without the internet, Business Standard noted. The 80 per cent problem Here is the uncomfortable part. An unnamed official claimed some Indian models now reach up to 80 per cent of what the world’s best models can do. No test or benchmark was named, so we cannot check that number. Even if it is true, think about what 80 per cent means. For writing a school essay, it is fine. For a defence analyst summarising intelligence reports, the missing 20 per cent is where mistakes hide. A wrong summary in a military office is far more dangerous than a data leak that never happens. So the risk does not disappear. It changes shape. We stop worrying about who can see our data and start worrying about whether the answer is right. “An Indian brain running on American chips is still a borrowed body.” The chips are still foreign An AI model is software. It needs powerful computer chips to run. In March, Minister of State Jitin Prasada told the Lok Sabha that more than 38,000 of these chips, called GPUs, had been added to the mission’s shared computing pool. A July report in Communications Today said most of them are Nvidia H100 and H200 units. Nvidia is an American company. This matters because chip sales are political. On 13 November, Reuters reported that US lawmakers are pushing for tougher controls on selling advanced AI chips abroad. The target is China, not India. Still, it is a reminder that the tap for these chips sits in Washington. A made-in-India model does not change that. Money is also moving slowly. Government figures given in the Rajya Sabha, as reported by MediaNama, showed ₹379 crore released in 2025-26 against a revised estimate of ₹800 crore. As of April, nothing had been released from this year’s ₹1,000 crore budget. Will it understand Kashmiri? For readers here, there is a more local question. Indian AI is sold as AI that understands Indian languages. But most of the attention goes to Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and Marathi. Kashmiri work has mostly come from small efforts. NIT Srinagar’s Gaash Lab ran a national challenge in August to build English-to-Kashmiri translation tools, Kashmir Life reported. AI4Bharat has put a Kashmiri speech-recognition model on the government’s AIKosh platform. And a young developer from Pulwama, Saqlain Yousuf, built a Kashmiri chatbot on his own, without funding, as this newspaper reported in February 2025. If government offices are later told to use only Indian models, people in Kashmir will deal with those systems for forms, complaints and services. A model that handles Hindi well but stumbles on Kashmiri is not much help in Pulwama or Baramulla. Bottom Line Wanting our own AI is sensible. But a rule that forces critical offices to switch before the tools are proven could swap one risk for another. Before any such order, the government should publish how these models perform on real tests, name which languages they truly support, and admit openly that the chips underneath still come from abroad. Sovereignty that only covers the software is half a job. The other half is the hardware underneath, and the languages people here actually speak. ( The author is studying Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence at Rutgers University, New Jersey, USA. He is interested in emerging technologies and innovation, and can be reached on LinkedIn at @arssh-kumar14)

A made-in-India model does not change that.

If government offices are later told to use only Indian models, people in Kashmir will deal with those systems for forms, complaints and services.
A model that handles Hindi well but stumbles on Kashmiri is not much help in Pulwama or Baramulla.

But a rule that forces critical offices to switch before the tools are proven could swap one risk for another.

Before any such order, the government should publish how these models perform on real tests, name which languages they truly support, and admit openly that the chips underneath still come from abroad.
Sovereignty that only covers the software is half a job.
The other half is the hardware underneath, and the languages people here actually speak.

stories.headline: Sand extraction surges 142% in J&K in one year
stories.title: Sand extraction surges 142% in J&K in one year
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 16: Sand and gravel extraction in Jammu and Kashmir increased by nearly 142 per cent, from 4.7 lakh tonnes in 2021 to 11.4 lakh tonnes in 2023, according to a research paper published in the Central University of Kashmir Law Review, which has raised concerns over the expansion of mechanised riverbed mining and its impact on Kashmir's rivers. The study, citing figures attributed to the Jammu and Kashmir Department of Geology and Mining, states that extraction rose from approximately 0.47 million tonnes to 1.14 million tonnes during the period, with 72 mining blocks reported as having been put up for auction. The increase of 6.7 lakh tonnes represents a 142.6 per cent rise over the earlier figure, pointing to a substantial expansion in the volume of riverbed material extracted. The findings form part of a research paper titled Illegal Sand Mining in River Jhelum in Jammu and Kashmir: Environmental Law and Governance Challenges, published in Central University of Kashmir Law Review. Authored by Syedah Fatima Zahara Jafri, Syed Irfan Haider Jafri and Mirza Juned Beg, the paper examines changes in mineral extraction, environmental damage and weaknesses in the regulation of mining activities along the Jhelum and its tributaries. The researchers observe that sand and gravel extraction in Kashmir has undergone a major change, moving from small-scale manual collection by local communities to commercial operations involving heavy machinery. The paper traces this transition to growing demand for construction materials, expansion of infrastructure projects and changes in the allocation of mining leases. It states that the widening of the Srinagar–Jammu National Highway and the construction of bridges, tunnels and other infrastructure increased demand for sand, gravel and crushed stone, encouraging the expansion of mechanised extraction. According to the study, traditional extraction practices were generally seasonal and limited in scale, while commercial operations introduced excavators, dredgers and large vehicles capable of removing substantially greater quantities of material. The researchers also refer to an earlier expansion in the number of mineral blocks offered for auction. Citing an auction status report attributed to the Department of Geology and Mining, the paper states that more than 100 minor-mineral blocks had been offered for open bidding by 2019–20. It identifies Pulwama, Budgam and Kulgam among the districts where mechanised extraction has been associated with riverbank erosion and instability. According to the researchers, the removal of sand and gravel at excessive depths can alter river channels, disturb sediment movement and weaken the natural support of riverbanks. The paper also raises concerns about the effects of deep excavation on groundwater recharge, irrigation systems and aquatic habitats. It cites a 2023 report attributed to the University of Kashmir's Environmental Policy Group, which associated mechanised excavation with a 15–18 per cent decline in groundwater levels in affected areas of Pulwama and Budgam. The researchers further identify the loss of fish breeding grounds and damage to wetlands as consequences of changes in riverbeds and sediment distribution. The study refers to environmental concerns in the Rambiara and Veshaw rivers, where deep excavation has been linked to damage to aquatic habitats. It also points to reports of declining water quality and the drying of traditional springs in mining-affected areas. While the increase in extraction reflects the growing demand for construction materials, the researchers question whether environmental monitoring and enforcement have kept pace with the expansion of mining activity. The paper observes that mining leases are subject to environmental clearances and restrictions intended to protect riverbanks, embankments and nearby infrastructure. However, it cites reports of extraction at night, use of heavy machinery near sensitive river stretches and operations outside approved mining areas. The researchers identify inadequate monitoring and poor coordination among departments as major weaknesses in the implementation of mining regulations. They argue that environmental safeguards must be assessed not only at the time mining leases are issued but throughout the period of extraction. The study recommends the use of GPS-based monitoring, digital records of mineral transportation and regular inspections to detect excavation beyond approved limits. It also calls for environmental assessments that examine the cumulative impact of mining on groundwater, fisheries, agriculture and flood vulnerability. The researchers maintain that greater public access to mining and environmental compliance records would help improve accountability. They also recommend involving local communities in monitoring riverbed extraction and reporting suspected violations.

stories.headline: India's CAD may touch 1.2% of GDP in FY27
stories.title: India's CAD may touch 1.2% of GDP in FY27
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: New Delhi: India's current account deficit (CAD) could remain close to 1.2 per cent of GDP in FY27, but sustained high crude oil prices and seasonal gold demand could put pressure on the country's external balance, according to a report by Union Bank of India.

The bank said the outlook for India's current account and overall balance of payments remained uncertain, with oil prices, services exports and gold imports likely to determine the extent of external sector pressure in the coming months.
"Though upside risks to CAD come from further gold buying during festive season; relief in crude prices in the H2 FY 27 could somewhat ease-out import pressures," the report said.

The caution comes after India's merchandise trade deficit widened to a 12-month high of USD 39.88 billion in October, from USD 30.21 billion in September, as imports rose to a record USD 89.35 billion.
Exports increased to USD 49.47 billion during the month.
The services trade surplus remained nearly flat at USD 19.8 billion, taking the overall trade deficit to USD 20.09 billion from USD 11 billion in September.
Gold, non-oil non-gold and oil imports contributed to the widening merchandise deficit.
Gold import volumes rose to an estimated 69.4 metric tonnes in October from 23.4 metric tonnes in September, while the non-oil, non-gold deficit reached a record USD 19.9 billion.
Union Bank's CAD projection assumes crude oil prices in the range of USD 95-100 per barrel.
It estimated that every USD 10 per barrel movement in oil prices could affect India's annual current account balance by nearly USD 15 billion.

The report also flagged risks from volatile non-oil imports, supply disruptions and higher global bond yields, which could add pressure to the balance of payments as the impact of foreign currency non-resident deposit inflows narrows.
"We stay cautious regarding the C/A and overall Balance of Payments outlook for FY27," the bank said, identifying oil prices, services export trends and seasonal gold demand as key factors to watch.
